claims.text: A machine-learning predictive model using atomic-scale, compositional, and microstructural features can identify high-entropy alloys with low phonon thermal conductivity more accurately than conventional mean-field or empirical approaches.
Configurational entropy and local scattering centers are informative atomic-scale features for predicting phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys.
Arc melting followed by homogenizing annealing can produce a predominantly single-phase, chemically disordered high-entropy alloy microstructure.
The proposed model will use descriptors linked to configurational disorder and phonon scattering to rank candidate high-entropy alloys.
Vacuum measurement conditions mitigate convective contributions to thermal-conductivity measurements.
High configurational disorder in a single-phase high-entropy alloy enhances phonon scattering.
Features used by the predictive model can capture configurational disorder and its associated phonon scattering.
Enhanced phonon scattering caused by atomic-scale disorder reduces phonon thermal conductivity.
Local atomic arrangements and configurational entropy influence phonon propagation.
Capturing the influence of local atomic arrangements on phonon propagation allows the model to distinguish alloys with lower phonon thermal conductivity.
The proposed model will reduce prediction error by approximately 15–20% relative to traditional mean-field or empirical methods.
Reducing prediction error will make identification of low-phonon-thermal-conductivity alloys more reliable.
Current mean-field and empirical prediction methods do not fully incorporate the complexities of configurational disorder.
The predictive approach is applicable primarily to homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloys.
The model's accuracy may diminish for multiphase alloys or alloys with significant compositional segregation.
Variability in alloy microstructures and scale-up issues may alter the model's quantitative improvement.
Failure to reduce prediction error by at least approximately 15–20% relative to traditional methods would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure of model-selected alloys to exhibit significantly lower measured thermal conductivity than baseline samples would falsify the hypothesis.
